The Chariot ("Because I could not stop for Death")
by Emily Dickinson
The following poem is by Emily Dickinson (1890).

```passage
Because I could not stop for Death,
He kindly stopped for me;
The carriage held but just ourselves
And Immortality.

We slowly drove, he knew no haste,
And I had put away
My labor, and my leisure too,
For his civility.

We passed the school where children played,
Their lessons scarcely done;
We passed the fields of gazing grain,
We passed the setting sun.

We paused before a house that seemed
A swelling of the ground;
The roof was scarcely visible,
The cornice but a mound.

Since then 't is centuries; but each
Feels shorter than the day
I first surmised the horses' heads
Were toward eternity.
```

text_map.central_idea: Speaking from centuries after her death, the speaker remembers dying as a polite, unhurried carriage ride with a courteous Death. The ride passes images of a whole life and stops at a grave described as a sunken house. Only at the end does she reveal that she slowly realized the ride led to eternity. The calm, mannerly surface keeps death's finality half-hidden until the last stanza.
text_map.speaker_or_narrator: A first-person speaker who has died. She looks back from an eternity that has lasted 'centuries' to the day Death called for her. She was Death's passenger and, in effect, the woman he was courting.

Public-domain source text — Gerard Manley Hopkins, God's Grandeur, Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins, ed. Robert Bridges (1918, first edition)
God's Grandeur
by Gerard Manley Hopkins
The following poem is by Gerard Manley Hopkins (1918).

```passage
THE world is charged with the grandeur of God.
   It will flame out, like shining from shook foil;
   It gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil
Crushed. Why do men then now not reck his rod?
Generations have trod, have trod, have trod;
   And all is seared with trade; bleared, smeared with toil;
   And wears man's smudge and shares man's smell: the soil
Is bare now, nor can foot feel, being shod.

And for all this, nature is never spent;
   There lives the dearest freshness deep down things;
And though the last lights off the black West went
   Oh, morning, at the brown brink eastward, springs--
Because the Holy Ghost over the bent
   World broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings.
```

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
The following poem is "God's Grandeur" by Gerard Manley Hopkins (1918). In this poem, the speaker reflects on a world filled with divine energy that generations of human labor and indifference have dulled, and then turns to a freshness that he insists keeps renewing it.

Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Gerard Manley Hopkins uses poetic elements and techniques to convey the speaker's tension between dismay at how humanity has worn down and ignored a divinely charged world and his confident faith that this divine presence keeps renewing the world anyway.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
- Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
Hopkins's "God's Grandeur" could be read as a simple before-and-after: eight lines of complaint about a ruined world, then six lines of comfort. But the poem doesn't let its comfort erase its grief. The octave's sounds grind and repeat like the labor they describe. The sestet's images place God's renewal "deep down" and inside a "bent" world. Through both, Hopkins suggests that divine presence does not undo human damage but works beneath and through it. The speaker's faith sounds confident because he has looked hard at the smudge first.

Even the opening praise contains pressure. "Charged" suggests electricity, but it can also mean something handed to someone as a duty, as if the world has been entrusted to us. Both similes show grandeur appearing only when something is disturbed. Foil has to be "shook" to flash, and oil gathers only after it is "Crushed," a word Hopkins strands at the start of line 4 so it lands with a thud. From the start, then, greatness comes out of force applied to matter. That makes the next question sound almost bewildered: "Why do men then now not reck his rod?" The run of stressed monosyllables, "men then now not," stumbles, as if the speaker can't get the question out smoothly.

The rest of the octave turns sound into argument. "Generations have trod, have trod, have trod" repeats the same flat beat three times, so the reader actually feels the monotony of centuries of feet. The internal rhymes "seared," "bleared," "smeared" pile up like layers of grime, and in "man's smudge and shares man's smell" the m and sh sounds smear into each other. Then Hopkins ends on the shoe: the foot, "being shod," cannot feel the soil. This is the subtlest loss in the poem. People haven't just damaged the earth. They have insulated themselves from it, so the charge of line 1 can't reach them anymore. His dismay is less about pollution than about numbness.

The sestet begins "And for all this," and the phrase matters. Hopkins doesn't pretend nothing happened; "for all this" admits every line before it. Renewal comes in spite of the damage, not by ignoring it. Even "nature is never spent" has a double meaning, since "spent" means both exhausted and paid out like money, so the language of "trade" gets turned against itself. The freshness lives "deep down things," below the surface where the smudge sits, and the soft d's of "dearest" and "deep down" ease the octave's harsh consonants into something gentler. The dawn image follows the same pattern. "The last lights off the black West went" sinks under its heavy monosyllables, but morning "springs" at the "brown brink." Brown is not a clean color. The new day rises out of the same soiled earth.

The final image completes this logic. The Holy Ghost broods over "the bent / World," and "bent" works two ways: the world is warped by toil, but it is also curved like an egg beneath a bird. The line break makes us feel the bend before we reach "World." "Broods" also means both to sit warmly on eggs and to worry, so even God's care keeps a trace of concern. In "God's Grandeur," Gerard Manley Hopkins shows a speaker who is upset by what people have done to the world but still sure that God keeps it alive. Hopkins builds this through the structure of the poem, moving from a harsh, heavy first section to a lighter, more hopeful second one, so that the faith in the end answers the dismay at the beginning instead of just ignoring it.

The poem begins with images of energy. The world "is charged with the grandeur of God," and the speaker compares this to "shining from shook foil" and to oil that gathers when it is "Crushed." These similes make God's presence seem like something that bursts out suddenly, and the word "Crushed" suggests that even pressure can bring out greatness. But right after this the tone changes with the question "Why do men then now not reck his rod?" The question is abrupt and sounds frustrated, as if the speaker cannot understand why people ignore something so obvious.

The next lines show the dismay most clearly. The repetition of "have trod, have trod, have trod" makes the line feel slow and heavy, like feet walking the same ground over and over. The sound of the words also matters. Words like "seared," "bleared," and "smeared" all rhyme and are crowded together, so the line feels messy and clogged, just like the world is described as being covered in "man's smudge" and "man's smell." Hopkins also says the soil is "bare" and that people cannot "feel, being shod." This image shows that people have lost touch with nature because of their shoes, which stand for the way work and trade separate them from the earth. The octave therefore uses sound and repetition to make the reader feel how worn out everything has become.

The poem turns with "And for all this, nature is never spent." This line admits the damage but refuses to give up on the world. The example of the morning that "springs" after the "black West" shows renewal in a natural cycle, because even when the last lights are gone, the sun comes back. The verb "springs" is quick and lively, which is a big contrast to the slow "trod."

The poem ends with the Holy Ghost who "broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings." This image of a bird protecting its young makes God seem caring and gentle, not just powerful like the "rod" earlier. The exclamation "ah!" shows the speaker is moved and excited, so the faith feels real and not just stated.

stanzas: THE world is charged with the grandeur of God.
It will flame out, like shining from shook foil;
It gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil
Crushed. Why do men then now not reck his rod?
Generations have trod, have trod, have trod;
And all is seared with trade; bleared, smeared with toil;

There lives the dearest freshness deep down things;
And though the last lights off the black West went

Because the Holy Ghost over the bent
World broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings.

Even "nature is never spent" has a double meaning, since "spent" means both exhausted and paid out like money, so the language of "trade" gets turned against itself. The freshness lives "deep down things," below the surface where the smudge sits, and the soft d's of "dearest" and "deep down" ease the octave's harsh consonants into something gentler. The dawn image follows the same pattern. "The last lights off the black West went" sinks under its heavy monosyllables, but morning "springs" at the "brown brink." Brown is not a clean color. The new day rises out of the same soiled earth.

The final image completes this logic. The Holy Ghost broods over "the bent / World," and "bent" works two ways: the world is warped by toil, but it is also curved like an egg beneath a bird. The line break makes us feel the bend before we reach "World." "Broods" also means both to sit warmly on eggs and to worry, so even God's care keeps a trace of concern. Then comes "ah!" in the middle of the line, as if the speaker suddenly sees the wings and is caught off guard. That small cry shows his faith isn't calm doctrine recited over the problem but something that happens to him as he looks.

The poem's confidence feels earned because Hopkins never claims the world is clean. The grandeur is crushed out like oil, the morning springs from a brown brink, and the Spirit's wings cover a bent World. For this speaker, renewal is not an escape from human failure but the one thing that goes deeper than it.

samples.essay:
In "God's Grandeur," Gerard Manley Hopkins shows a speaker who is upset by what people have done to the world but still sure that God keeps it alive. Hopkins builds this through the structure of the poem, moving from a harsh, heavy first section to a lighter, more hopeful second one, so that the faith in the end answers the dismay at the beginning instead of just ignoring it.

The poem begins with images of energy. The world "is charged with the grandeur of God," and the speaker compares this to "shining from shook foil" and to oil that gathers when it is "Crushed." These similes make God's presence seem like something that bursts out suddenly, and the word "Crushed" suggests that even pressure can bring out greatness. But right after this the tone changes with the question "Why do men then now not reck his rod?" The question is abrupt and sounds frustrated, as if the speaker cannot understand why people ignore something so obvious.

The next lines show the dismay most clearly. The repetition of "have trod, have trod, have trod" makes the line feel slow and heavy, like feet walking the same ground over and over. The sound of the words also matters. Words like "seared," "bleared," and "smeared" all rhyme and are crowded together, so the line feels messy and clogged, just like the world is described as being covered in "man's smudge" and "man's smell." Hopkins also says the soil is "bare" and that people cannot "feel, being shod." This image shows that people have lost touch with nature because of their shoes, which stand for the way work and trade separate them from the earth. The octave therefore uses sound and repetition to make the reader feel how worn out everything has become.

The poem turns with "And for all this, nature is never spent." This line admits the damage but refuses to give up on the world. The images become much softer and more hopeful, with "the dearest freshness deep down things." The word "deep" suggests that the goodness is hidden below the surface where human toil cannot reach. The example of the morning that "springs" after the "black West" shows renewal in a natural cycle, because even when the last lights are gone, the sun comes back. The verb "springs" is quick and lively, which is a big contrast to the slow "trod."

The poem ends with the Holy Ghost who "broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings." This image of a bird protecting its young makes God seem caring and gentle, not just powerful like the "rod" earlier. The exclamation "ah!" shows the speaker is moved and excited, so the faith feels real and not just stated.

Overall, Hopkins uses sound, repetition, and imagery to show both sides of the speaker's feelings. The harsh sounds of the first half show how humans have damaged the world, and the warmer images of the second half show that God's renewal is stronger.

The Lady with the Dog
by Anton Chekhov, translated by Constance Garnett
The following passage from a short story is by Anton Chekhov, translated by Constance Garnett (1917). This is an excerpt.

```passage
    IT was said that a new person had appeared on the
sea-front: a lady with a little dog. Dmitri Dmitritch
Gurov, who had by then been a fortnight at Yalta, and so
was fairly at home there, had begun to take an interest
in new arrivals. Sitting in Verney's pavilion, he saw,
walking on the sea-front, a fair-haired young lady of
medium height, wearing a béret; a white Pomeranian dog
was running behind her.

    And afterwards he met her in the public gardens and
in the square several times a day. She was walking
alone, always wearing the same béret, and always with
the same white dog; no one knew who she was, and every
one called her simply "the lady with the dog."

    "If she is here alone without a husband or friends,
it wouldn't be amiss to make her acquaintance," Gurov
reflected.

    He was under forty, but he had a daughter already
twelve years old, and two sons at school. He had been
married young, when he was a student in his second year,
and by now his wife seemed half as old again as he. She
was a tall, erect woman with dark eyebrows, staid and
dignified, and, as she said of herself, intellectual.
She read a great deal, used phonetic spelling, called
her husband, not Dmitri, but Dimitri, and he secretly
considered her unintelligent, narrow, inelegant, was
afraid of her, and did not like to be at home. He had
begun being unfaithful to her long ago--had been
unfaithful to her often, and, probably on that account,
almost always spoke ill of women, and when they were
talked about in his presence, used to call them "the
lower race."

    It seemed to him that he had been so schooled by
bitter experience that he might call them what he liked,
and yet he could not get on for two days together
without "the lower race." In the society of men he was
bored and not himself, with them he was cold and
uncommunicative; but when he was in the company of women
he felt free, and knew what to say to them and how to
behave; and he was at ease with them even when he was
silent. In his appearance, in his character, in his
whole nature, there was something attractive and elusive
which allured women and disposed them in his favour; he
knew that, and some force seemed to draw him, too, to
them.

    Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience,
had taught him long ago that with decent people,
especially Moscow people--always slow to move and
irresolute--every intimacy, which at first so agreeably
diversifies life and appears a light and charming
adventure, inevitably grows into a regular problem of
extreme intricacy, and in the long run the situation
becomes unbearable. But at every fresh meeting with an
interesting woman this experience seemed to slip out of
his memory, and he was eager for life, and everything
seemed simple and amusing.

    One evening he was dining in the gardens, and the
lady in the béret came up slowly to take the next table.
Her expression, her gait, her dress, and the way she did
her hair told him that she was a lady, that she was
married, that she was in Yalta for the first time and
alone, and that she was dull there.... The stories told
of the immorality in such places as Yalta are to a great
extent untrue; he despised them, and knew that such
stories were for the most part made up by persons who
would themselves have been glad to sin if they had been
able; but when the lady sat down at the next table three
paces from him, he remembered these tales of easy
conquests, of trips to the mountains, and the tempting
thought of a swift, fleeting love affair, a romance with
an unknown woman, whose name he did not know, suddenly
took possession of him.

    He beckoned coaxingly to the Pomeranian, and when
the dog came up to him he shook his finger at it. The
Pomeranian growled: Gurov shook his finger at it again.
```

parts.prompt:
The following passage is from "The Lady with the Dog," a short story by Anton Chekhov (1899 in the original; English translation by Constance Garnett, 1917). In this passage, the narrator introduces Dmitri Dmitritch Gurov, a married man on holiday at Yalta, as he notices a young woman walking alone with a small white dog and begins to imagine an affair with her.

Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Anton Chekhov uses literary elements and techniques to portray Gurov as a man whose claimed worldly experience and scorn for women are undercut by his dependence on them and his readiness to forget what experience has taught him.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
- Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
Gurov thinks of himself as a man who has seen through women, but Chekhov's narrator stays just close enough to his thoughts to show that the contempt is a cover. Using a close, half-ironic narrative voice, sentences that turn on "and yet" and "but," and a final comic moment with a dog, Chekhov presents Gurov's "bitter experience" as a lesson he keeps repeating and keeps forgetting. Still, the narrator never simply sneers at him. By paying attention to his loveless marriage and his loneliness among men, Chekhov makes Gurov ridiculous and believable at once.

The irony starts with how Gurov's opinions are framed. The narrator tells us he called women "the lower race," but the explanation comes from the narrator: he was unfaithful often, and "probably on that account" spoke ill of women. That small phrase flips the cause and effect Gurov would claim. He doesn't scorn women because experience taught him to. He scorns them because he has wronged them and needs a reason. The next paragraph opens with "It seemed to him," which marks his sense of being "schooled" as his own belief, not a fact the narrator confirms. Then the sentence pivots: he could call them what he liked, "and yet he could not get on for two days together" without them. The grammar acts out the contradiction, with the boast in the first half and the dependence in the second.

Chekhov does not let the irony go cold, though. The description of Gurov's wife cuts both ways. She is "intellectual" only "as she said of herself," which mocks her pretensions, and Gurov privately judges her "unintelligent, narrow, inelegant." But the list ends with "was afraid of her, and did not like to be at home." The last item gives him away, because a man who fears his wife is not the master of women he imagines. The same goes for the line that among men he is "bored and not himself," while with women "he felt free." These details make his chasing less like conquest and more like a hunt for the only place he can be himself, so the reader pities him even while seeing through him.

The paragraph about experience repeats its lesson in the way it is built. "Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience" is insistent, almost exhausted, as if Gurov is trying to drill the lesson into himself. The long sentence that follows moves from "a light and charming adventure" to "a regular problem of extreme intricacy," and its piled-up clauses feel as tangled as the affairs it describes. Then one short "But" wipes the lesson away: the experience "seemed to slip out of his memory." The verb is passive. Gurov doesn't choose to forget, it just happens to him, the same way "some force seemed to draw him" and the thought of an affair "suddenly took possession of him." Chekhov lets Gurov feel like the victim of his own desire, but the repeated "seemed" keeps that excuse at a distance. The Yalta gossip works the same way. Gurov despises the storytellers as people "who would themselves have been glad to sin," which describes him exactly, and a sentence later "he remembered these tales." His scorn and his temptation sit inside one sentence.

The ending shrinks this whole pattern down to a gesture. The woman has no name. She is "the lady with the dog," and Gurov reads her gait and dress as signs that she is married, alone and "dull," confident in his worldly expertise. What attracts him is a woman "whose name he did not know," in other words someone he can't really know. Then he beckons "coaxingly" to the Pomeranian, shakes his finger at it, and when "The Pomeranian growled," he does it again. Coaxing, scolding and trying again regardless is exactly how he treats women, and the growl is a warning he ignores just as he ignores his experience. It is funny, but it also suggests that Gurov, for all his claims, has learned nothing at all.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis must make an interpretive claim about how the passage presents Gurov, and it must deal with the tension between what he says or believes (his contempt for women, his bitter experience, his scorn of Yalta gossip) and what he feels or does (needing women, forgetting his lessons, being carried away by the thought of an affair). Acceptable theses might say the narrator ironically exposes Gurov's contempt as a defense that hides his dependence, or that the passage shows a man trapped in a repeating cycle of disillusionment and renewed appetite, or that Chekhov's mix of detachment and sympathy makes Gurov both ridiculous and human. A thesis that only restates the prompt, only lists devices, only summarizes (for example, 'Gurov sees a lady and wants to meet her'), or only judges Gurov morally ('Gurov is a bad husband') without a claim about how he is portrayed does not earn the point.

Strong responses build a line of reasoning from specific textual details. Key evidence includes the reversal in 'he might call them what he liked, and yet he could not get on for two days together without "the lower race"'; the repeated 'Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience' set against 'this experience seemed to slip out of his memory'; the movement from 'a light and charming adventure' to 'a regular problem of extreme intricacy'; the ironic 'as she said of herself, intellectual' and the list of 'unintelligent, narrow, inelegant, was afraid of her'; his scorn for gossips 'who would themselves have been glad to sin' just before the same tales tempt him; the passive phrasing 'some force seemed to draw him' and 'suddenly took possession of him'; and the closing moment with the growling Pomeranian. Commentary has to explain how these choices show the gap between Gurov's self-image and his behavior, for example how the narrator's close, half-ironic voice ('It seemed to him') lets readers see past his own rationalizations. A score of 4 needs consistent, specific commentary that ties evidence to the thesis across the passage. A score of 3 explains several pieces of evidence well but unevenly. A score of 2 relies on summary, or names devices with little explanation. A score of 1 or 0 is mostly paraphrase or uses evidence that has nothing to do with the claim.

Sophistication can be earned by tracing the complexity in how the narrator treats Gurov, who is mocked and also understood: the irony exposes his hypocrisy while the attention to his boredom with men and his marriage makes his longing believable. It can also be earned by showing how the passage's own structure acts out the cycle it describes, with a lesson stated and then immediately forgotten. Other routes are reading the final gesture with the dog as a small comic model of his whole approach to women (coaxing, then scolding, then repeating), or noting how the lady is reduced to a label and a set of readable signs ('the lady with the dog', 'whose name he did not know') in a way that shows how Gurov sees women. The point goes to responses that develop one of these readings throughout the essay. Passing mentions or sweeping claims about Chekhov or human nature do not earn it.

In this passage from "The Lady with the Dog," Chekhov shows Gurov as a man who believes he is experienced and above women, but whose behavior proves the opposite. Through irony and a narrator who stays close to Gurov's thoughts while still pointing out his contradictions, Chekhov makes Gurov both a little ridiculous and believable, a man who says one thing and does another.

The clearest contradiction is in how Gurov talks about women. The narrator says he "almost always spoke ill of women" and called them "the lower race." This sounds like contempt, but the next paragraph undercuts it. It says "It seemed to him that he had been so schooled by bitter experience that he might call them what he liked." The phrase "It seemed to him" shows that this is only Gurov's opinion of himself, and the narrator does not agree with it. Then comes the reversal, "yet he could not get on for two days together" without them. The word "yet" turns the sentence around, so the reader sees that the name-calling is not real superiority. He actually needs women, since with men he is "bored and not himself" but with women he feels "free." So his scorn seems more like a cover for dependence.

Chekhov also uses repetition to show how Gurov forgets what he has learned. The narrator writes "Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience," which makes the lesson sound heavy and serious. The lesson is that affairs start as "a light and charming adventure" and end as "a regular problem of extreme intricacy." The contrast between "light and charming" and "extreme intricacy" shows how much trouble he knows is coming. But then "this experience seemed to slip out of his memory," and "everything seemed simple and amusing." The structure of the passage acts this out, because the lesson is stated and then forgotten right away, just as Gurov forgets it with every new woman.

The description of his wife adds to this. She is described as "as she said of herself, intellectual," which is ironic because it is her own claim, and the details that follow, like phonetic spelling, make it seem silly. Gurov thinks she is "unintelligent, narrow, inelegant" and he is "afraid of her." The list shows his dislike, but being afraid shows he is not as strong as he pretends. This helps explain why he looks for other women, and it makes the reader understand him a bit.

Finally, the passage ends with Gurov teasing the dog. He first calls the gossip about Yalta untrue and says people who spread it "would themselves have been glad to sin," but then he remembers the same tales and the thought of an affair "suddenly took possession of him." The passive wording makes it seem like he has no control. The ending, where he shakes his finger at the growling Pomeranian twice, is a small version of the whole thing, since he does it again even after the dog growls.

Overall, Chekhov uses irony, repetition, and the narrator's tone to show that Gurov's experience and scorn are not as strong as he thinks, and that his desire wins over what he knows.

lit_frq.title: Prose Fiction Analysis: The Lady with the Dog

prompt.lead: The following passage is from "The Lady with the Dog," a short story by Anton Chekhov (1899 in the original; English translation by Constance Garnett, 1917). In this passage, the narrator introduces Dmitri Dmitritch Gurov, a married man on holiday at Yalta, as he notices a young woman walking alone with a small white dog and begins to imagine an affair with her.
prompt.task: Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Anton Chekhov uses literary elements and techniques to portray Gurov as a man whose claimed worldly experience and scorn for women are undercut by his dependence on them and his readiness to forget what experience has taught him.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

passage.title: The Lady with the Dog
passage.attribution: by Anton Chekhov, translated by Constance Garnett
passage.headnote: The following passage from a short story is by Anton Chekhov, translated by Constance Garnett (1917). This is an excerpt.
stanzas: IT was said that a new person had appeared on the
sea-front: a lady with a little dog. Dmitri Dmitritch
Gurov, who had by then been a fortnight at Yalta, and so
was fairly at home there, had begun to take an interest
in new arrivals. Sitting in Verney's pavilion, he saw,
walking on the sea-front, a fair-haired young lady of
medium height, wearing a béret; a white Pomeranian dog
was running behind her.
And afterwards he met her in the public gardens and
in the square several times a day. She was walking
alone, always wearing the same béret, and always with
the same white dog; no one knew who she was, and every
one called her simply "the lady with the dog."
"If she is here alone without a husband or friends,
it wouldn't be amiss to make her acquaintance," Gurov
reflected.
He was under forty, but he had a daughter already
twelve years old, and two sons at school. He had been
married young, when he was a student in his second year,
and by now his wife seemed half as old again as he. She
was a tall, erect woman with dark eyebrows, staid and
dignified, and, as she said of herself, intellectual.
She read a great deal, used phonetic spelling, called
her husband, not Dmitri, but Dimitri, and he secretly
considered her unintelligent, narrow, inelegant, was
afraid of her, and did not like to be at home. He had
begun being unfaithful to her long ago--had been
unfaithful to her often, and, probably on that account,
almost always spoke ill of women, and when they were
talked about in his presence, used to call them "the
lower race."
It seemed to him that he had been so schooled by
bitter experience that he might call them what he liked,
and yet he could not get on for two days together
without "the lower race." In the society of men he was
bored and not himself, with them he was cold and
uncommunicative; but when he was in the company of women
he felt free, and knew what to say to them and how to
behave; and he was at ease with them even when he was
silent. In his appearance, in his character, in his
whole nature, there was something attractive and elusive
which allured women and disposed them in his favour; he
knew that, and some force seemed to draw him, too, to
them.
Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience,
had taught him long ago that with decent people,
especially Moscow people--always slow to move and
irresolute--every intimacy, which at first so agreeably
diversifies life and appears a light and charming
adventure, inevitably grows into a regular problem of
extreme intricacy, and in the long run the situation
becomes unbearable. But at every fresh meeting with an
interesting woman this experience seemed to slip out of
his memory, and he was eager for life, and everything
seemed simple and amusing.
One evening he was dining in the gardens, and the
lady in the béret came up slowly to take the next table.
Her expression, her gait, her dress, and the way she did
her hair told him that she was a lady, that she was
married, that she was in Yalta for the first time and
alone, and that she was dull there.... The stories told
of the immorality in such places as Yalta are to a great
extent untrue; he despised them, and knew that such
stories were for the most part made up by persons who
would themselves have been glad to sin if they had been
able; but when the lady sat down at the next table three
paces from him, he remembered these tales of easy
conquests, of trips to the mountains, and the tempting
thought of a swift, fleeting love affair, a romance with
an unknown woman, whose name he did not know, suddenly
took possession of him.
He beckoned coaxingly to the Pomeranian, and when
the dog came up to him he shook his finger at it. The
Pomeranian growled: Gurov shook his finger at it again.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.task_specific: A defensible thesis must make an interpretive claim about how the passage presents Gurov, and it must deal with the tension between what he says or believes (his contempt for women, his bitter experience, his scorn of Yalta gossip) and what he feels or does (needing women, forgetting his lessons, being carried away by the thought of an affair). Acceptable theses might say the narrator ironically exposes Gurov's contempt as a defense that hides his dependence, or that the passage shows a man trapped in a repeating cycle of disillusionment and renewed appetite, or that Chekhov's mix of detachment and sympathy makes Gurov both ridiculous and human. A thesis that only restates the prompt, only lists devices, only summarizes (for example, 'Gurov sees a lady and wants to meet her'), or only judges Gurov morally ('Gurov is a bad husband') without a claim about how he is portrayed does not earn the point.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.task_specific: Strong responses build a line of reasoning from specific textual details. Key evidence includes the reversal in 'he might call them what he liked, and yet he could not get on for two days together without "the lower race"'; the repeated 'Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience' set against 'this experience seemed to slip out of his memory'; the movement from 'a light and charming adventure' to 'a regular problem of extreme intricacy'; the ironic 'as she said of herself, intellectual' and the list of 'unintelligent, narrow, inelegant, was afraid of her'; his scorn for gossips 'who would themselves have been glad to sin' just before the same tales tempt him; the passive phrasing 'some force seemed to draw him' and 'suddenly took possession of him'; and the closing moment with the growling Pomeranian. Commentary has to explain how these choices show the gap between Gurov's self-image and his behavior, for example how the narrator's close, half-ironic voice ('It seemed to him') lets readers see past his own rationalizations. A score of 4 needs consistent, specific commentary that ties evidence to the thesis across the passage. A score of 3 explains several pieces of evidence well but unevenly. A score of 2 relies on summary, or names devices with little explanation. A score of 1 or 0 is mostly paraphrase or uses evidence that has nothing to do with the claim.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication can be earned by tracing the complexity in how the narrator treats Gurov, who is mocked and also understood: the irony exposes his hypocrisy while the attention to his boredom with men and his marriage makes his longing believable. It can also be earned by showing how the passage's own structure acts out the cycle it describes, with a lesson stated and then immediately forgotten. Other routes are reading the final gesture with the dog as a small comic model of his whole approach to women (coaxing, then scolding, then repeating), or noting how the lady is reduced to a label and a set of readable signs ('the lady with the dog', 'whose name he did not know') in a way that shows how Gurov sees women. The point goes to responses that develop one of these readings throughout the essay. Passing mentions or sweeping claims about Chekhov or human nature do not earn it.

scoring_notes: Do not require or reward knowledge of later events in the story; responses must be grounded in this passage.
Moral condemnation of Gurov is acceptable only when it is tied to analysis of how the text presents him; disapproval alone is not analysis.
Do not credit readings that assume the narrator agrees with calling women 'the lower race' unless the response deals with the irony around that phrase.
Device identification without explanation of effect should not move a response above 2 in Row B.
Accept a range of interpretations of the dog ending (comic, symbolic, foreshadowing a pattern) as long as they are supported.

defensible_positions: The narrator's irony exposes Gurov's contempt for women as hypocritical and self-protective: he calls them 'the lower race' yet cannot do without them and feels like himself only in their company.
The passage presents Gurov as caught in a repeating cycle in which hard-won experience is forgotten at every new encounter, so his worldliness looks less like wisdom and more like self-deception.
Gurov is shown as oddly passive in his own desires, drawn by 'some force' and taken over by a 'tempting thought', which makes him both less responsible and less in control than he thinks.

Chekhov balances judgment with sympathy: the unhappy marriage, the fear of his wife, and his boredom with men make Gurov's restlessness understandable even while the narrator mocks his rationalizations.

Gurov's habit of reading women as types (decoding the lady's dress and gait, choosing her because she is nameless and unknown) shows how he turns women into objects of his own story, a habit the growling dog comically pushes back against.

samples.essay:
Gurov thinks of himself as a man who has seen through women, but Chekhov's narrator stays just close enough to his thoughts to show that the contempt is a cover. Using a close, half-ironic narrative voice, sentences that turn on "and yet" and "but," and a final comic moment with a dog, Chekhov presents Gurov's "bitter experience" as a lesson he keeps repeating and keeps forgetting. Still, the narrator never simply sneers at him. By paying attention to his loveless marriage and his loneliness among men, Chekhov makes Gurov ridiculous and believable at once.

The irony starts with how Gurov's opinions are framed. The narrator tells us he called women "the lower race," but the explanation comes from the narrator: he was unfaithful often, and "probably on that account" spoke ill of women. That small phrase flips the cause and effect Gurov would claim. He doesn't scorn women because experience taught him to. He scorns them because he has wronged them and needs a reason. The next paragraph opens with "It seemed to him," which marks his sense of being "schooled" as his own belief, not a fact the narrator confirms. Then the sentence pivots: he could call them what he liked, "and yet he could not get on for two days together" without them. The grammar acts out the contradiction, with the boast in the first half and the dependence in the second.

Chekhov does not let the irony go cold, though. The description of Gurov's wife cuts both ways. She is "intellectual" only "as she said of herself," which mocks her pretensions, and Gurov privately judges her "unintelligent, narrow, inelegant." But the list ends with "was afraid of her, and did not like to be at home." The last item gives him away, because a man who fears his wife is not the master of women he imagines. The same goes for the line that among men he is "bored and not himself," while with women "he felt free." These details make his chasing less like conquest and more like a hunt for the only place he can be himself, so the reader pities him even while seeing through him.

The paragraph about experience repeats its lesson in the way it is built. "Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience" is insistent, almost exhausted, as if Gurov is trying to drill the lesson into himself. The long sentence that follows moves from "a light and charming adventure" to "a regular problem of extreme intricacy," and its piled-up clauses feel as tangled as the affairs it describes. Then one short "But" wipes the lesson away: the experience "seemed to slip out of his memory." The verb is passive. Gurov doesn't choose to forget, it just happens to him, the same way "some force seemed to draw him" and the thought of an affair "suddenly took possession of him." Chekhov lets Gurov feel like the victim of his own desire, but the repeated "seemed" keeps that excuse at a distance. The Yalta gossip works the same way. Gurov despises the storytellers as people "who would themselves have been glad to sin," which describes him exactly, and a sentence later "he remembered these tales." His scorn and his temptation sit inside one sentence.

The ending shrinks this whole pattern down to a gesture. The woman has no name. She is "the lady with the dog," and Gurov reads her gait and dress as signs that she is married, alone and "dull," confident in his worldly expertise. What attracts him is a woman "whose name he did not know," in other words someone he can't really know. Then he beckons "coaxingly" to the Pomeranian, shakes his finger at it, and when "The Pomeranian growled," he does it again. Coaxing, scolding and trying again regardless is exactly how he treats women, and the growl is a warning he ignores just as he ignores his experience. It is funny, but it also suggests that Gurov, for all his claims, has learned nothing at all.

The clearest contradiction is in how Gurov talks about women. The narrator says he "almost always spoke ill of women" and called them "the lower race." This sounds like contempt, but the next paragraph undercuts it. It says "It seemed to him that he had been so schooled by bitter experience that he might call them what he liked." The phrase "It seemed to him" shows that this is only Gurov's opinion of himself, and the narrator does not agree with it. Then comes the reversal, "yet he could not get on for two days together" without them. The word "yet" turns the sentence around, so the reader sees that the name-calling is not real superiority. He actually needs women, since with men he is "bored and not himself" but with women he feels "free." So his scorn seems more like a cover for dependence.

Chekhov also uses repetition to show how Gurov forgets what he has learned. The narrator writes "Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience," which makes the lesson sound heavy and serious. The lesson is that affairs start as "a light and charming adventure" and end as "a regular problem of extreme intricacy." The contrast between "light and charming" and "extreme intricacy" shows how much trouble he knows is coming. But then "this experience seemed to slip out of his memory," and "everything seemed simple and amusing." The structure of the passage acts this out, because the lesson is stated and then forgotten right away, just as Gurov forgets it with every new woman.

The description of his wife adds to this. She is described as "as she said of herself, intellectual," which is ironic because it is her own claim, and the details that follow, like phonetic spelling, make it seem silly. Gurov thinks she is "unintelligent, narrow, inelegant" and he is "afraid of her." The list shows his dislike, but being afraid shows he is not as strong as he pretends. This helps explain why he looks for other women, and it makes the reader understand him a bit.

Finally, the passage ends with Gurov teasing the dog. He first calls the gossip about Yalta untrue and says people who spread it "would themselves have been glad to sin," but then he remembers the same tales and the thought of an affair "suddenly took possession of him." The passive wording makes it seem like he has no control. The ending, where he shakes his finger at the growling Pomeranian twice, is a small version of the whole thing, since he does it again even after the dog growls.

Overall, Chekhov uses irony, repetition, and the narrator's tone to show that Gurov's experience and scorn are not as strong as he thinks, and that his desire wins over what he knows.

samples.essay:
In the passage from "The Lady with the Dog," Chekhov shows Gurov as a man who has a lot of experience with women and who is also married. He sees a lady with a dog in Yalta and starts thinking about having an affair with her. This shows that Gurov is not a very good husband and that he does not respect women.

First, Chekhov tells us about Gurov's family. He has a daughter who is twelve and two sons at school. He married young and his wife seems older than him. She is described as "staid and dignified" and she says she is intellectual. Gurov does not like her and he does not like to be at home. This is why he has been unfaithful to her many times. The narrator also says he calls women "the lower race" which is a bad thing to say about women.

Next, the passage says that Gurov has had "bitter experience" with women. He thinks that affairs always become a problem in the end. But when he meets a new woman he forgets all of this and thinks everything is simple and amusing. So he does not really learn from what happened before. The narrator says it "seemed to slip out of his memory" which shows that he forgets.

Then the lady comes to sit at the next table at dinner. Gurov thinks about the stories of Yalta and gets tempted. At the end he calls the dog over and shakes his finger at it and the dog growls. This is a small moment but it shows he is trying to get close to the lady.

In conclusion, Chekhov uses details about Gurov's marriage and his thoughts to show that he says one thing about women but does another. He is a man who is unfaithful and forgets his lessons, which makes him seem like a bad person.

blueprint.central_idea: The opening of the story presents Gurov through a close, quietly ironic narration that sets his self-image as an experienced man who scorns women against his dependence on them, his fear of his wife, and his habit of forgetting every lesson when a new woman appears.
blueprint.complexity: The passage is neither a simple condemnation nor a simple endorsement. The narrator mocks Gurov's rationalizations and his hypocrisy toward the gossips, yet gives him an unhappy marriage, a believable loneliness, and a passivity before his desires that makes him human. The structure acts out the cycle it describes, and the comic gesture with the dog both sums up and deflates his practiced charm.
